terms.simple_def: When a private company first sells its shares to the public on the stock market.
A stage when investors give a startup money in exchange for owning part of it.
Investors who give money to young, risky companies hoping they grow very large.
Owning a part of a company, usually as shares.
How much money people agree a company is worth.
How many months a company can keep operating before its money runs out.
How much money a company spends each month beyond what it earns.
Money a company expects to earn every year from subscriptions.
Software you rent online by subscription instead of installing and owning it.
A company that sells to other companies, not to regular people.
The plan for how a product will reach and be sold to customers.
When many customers clearly want and pay for what you built.
How much value you get back compared with what you spent.
A number a team watches to see if it is reaching its goals.
A goal plus a few measurable results that show if the goal was met.
A person or group affected by a project who cares how it turns out.
A plan showing what a team will build and roughly when.
The simplest version of a product that real users can try.
When a company changes direction to a new product or market.
The share of customers who stop paying over a period.
A private startup valued at more than one billion dollars.
When one company buys another company.
Something that makes it hard for competitors to copy a company.
When switching away from a supplier is so hard or costly that you stay.
A small test to show an idea can work before building it fully.
Large companies, which usually need extra security, support, and contracts.
A written promise to customers about uptime or speed, often with penalties.
The main talk of a conference, usually given to everyone at once.
A smaller talk that runs at the same time as other talks.
The useful conversations people have between talks, outside the rooms.
A very short talk, usually five minutes or less.
The open request for people to submit talk ideas to a conference.
A company's stand at a conference where you can meet its team.
Free items companies give away, like stickers and t-shirts.
To return to a topic later.
To discuss something later, privately, not in the current meeting.
Send someone a short message.
Free time or energy to take on more work. In networks: how much data can move.
Easy tasks that give good results quickly.
To make a change big enough to notice.
To try to do far too much at once.
The basic features everyone expects; you need them just to compete.
When a company uses its own product every day.
The one number a team uses to judge if it is succeeding.
A long, detailed look at one topic.
A set of rules that lets one program ask another program for data or actions.
A package of tools and code that makes building on a platform easier.
Renting computers and storage over the internet instead of owning them.
A computer that runs programs and answers requests from other computers.
Organized storage for data that programs can search and update.
The delay between asking for something and getting the answer.
How much work a system finishes in a period of time.
The part of software that users see and touch.
The part of software that runs on servers, out of the user's sight.
Software whose code is public, so anyone can read, use, and change it.
The place where a project's code and its history are stored.
A tool that tracks every change to code and who made it.
A proposed code change that teammates review before it is accepted.
A saved snapshot of code changes, with a short message.
A separate copy of the code where you can work without affecting others.
Combining changes from one branch into another.
When teammates read your code changes to find problems before they ship.
Automatic testing and shipping of code every time someone changes it.
To put a new version of software where users can use it.
The live system that real users are using.
A copy of the live system for testing before release.
A mistake in software that makes it behave wrongly.
An urgent fix shipped quickly to repair a live problem.
Returning to the previous working version after a bad release.
Rewriting code to make it cleaner without changing what it does.
Shortcuts in code that save time now but cost more work later.
Old software that still runs but is hard to change.
One big application where all parts are built and deployed together.
Building an app as many small services that talk to each other.
Being able to handle more users or data without breaking.
A system that spreads incoming traffic across several servers.
A fast copy of data kept close by so it loads quicker.
Servers around the world that deliver files from a location near each user.
The internet's address book that turns website names into server addresses.
A message one app sends to another automatically when something happens.
Checking who you are, for example with a password.
Checking what you are allowed to do after you log in.
Scrambling data so only people with the right key can read it.
The share of time a system is working and available.
A period when a service is not working for users.
Running code without managing servers; the provider runs it only when needed.
A way of working in short cycles, delivering small pieces often.
A short fixed period, often two weeks, to finish a set of work.
A short daily team meeting to share progress and problems.
An unusual situation that software may not handle well.
When something that used to work breaks after a change.
A free, open-source operating system that runs most servers.
A simple text format for writing settings, used a lot in Kubernetes.
A common text format for sending structured data between programs.
Automatic steps that move and clean data from one place to another.
Happening right away, with almost no delay.
A design where parts of a system react when something happens.
A package holding an app and everything it needs, so it runs the same anywhere.
The most popular tool for building and running containers.
The saved template a container starts from.
A storage place for container images.
Open-source software that runs and manages many containers across many computers.
A group of computers working together as one system.
One computer, real or virtual, inside a cluster.
The smallest unit Kubernetes runs: one or a few containers together.
Kubernetes settings that keep a chosen number of copies of an app running.
A stable address in Kubernetes that sends traffic to the right pods.
Kubernetes rules for how outside web traffic reaches services inside the cluster.
A named area inside a cluster that keeps teams' resources separate.
A package manager for Kubernetes that installs apps with one command.
The command-line tool for talking to a Kubernetes cluster.
The brain of a Kubernetes cluster that decides where things run.
The database where Kubernetes stores the state of the cluster.
Software that automatically runs and repairs a complex app inside Kubernetes.
A way to add your own object types to Kubernetes.
A file, usually YAML, that describes what should run in Kubernetes.
Automatically adding or removing copies of an app as traffic changes.
One identical copy of an app or database.
A pod that keeps crashing and restarting, with longer waits between tries.
A container was stopped because it used more memory than allowed.
A helper container that runs next to the main app in the same pod.
A layer that controls, secures, and observes traffic between microservices.
A way to run small safe programs inside the Linux kernel to watch or control the system.
Managing systems by changing files in Git, which tools then apply automatically.
Creating servers and networks from code files instead of clicking in a console.
Using more than one cloud provider at the same time.
A team building shared tools so other developers can ship easily on their own.
Developers and operations working together to ship and run software faster.
Engineers who use software to keep live systems reliable and fast.
The nonprofit that hosts Kubernetes and many other open-source projects; it runs KubeCon.
Software designed from the start to run on cloud platforms in containers.
Any app or job running on a system.
Automatically starting, stopping, and placing many containers across machines.
Security that checks every request, never trusting anything just because it is inside.
Giving permissions to roles, then giving roles to people.
Safely storing passwords and keys that programs need.
Protecting all the code and tools your software is built from.
A list of every component inside a piece of software.
A publicly listed security weakness with an ID number.
A chip that does many calculations at once; it powers AI.
Being able to understand what a live system is doing from the data it sends out.
Watching a system's health and warning people when something looks wrong.
Data a system sends about itself: logs, metrics, and traces.
An open standard for collecting telemetry from any app.
A record of one request's full path through many services, with timing.
One timed step inside a trace.
Time-stamped text messages a program writes about what it did.
Numbers measured over time, like requests per second.
A screen of charts showing a system's health at a glance.
An automatic warning sent when something crosses a limit.
A measurement of how well a service works for users, like success rate.
A target for a reliability measurement, like 99.9% of requests succeed.
How much failure an SLO allows before the team must stop and fix reliability.
The time within which 99% of requests finish; the slowest 1% take longer.
The average time it takes to fix a problem.
An unplanned problem that hurts a service and needs a fast response.
Being the person who must respond if the system breaks, even at night.
Urgently alerting the on-call engineer by phone.
A written review after an incident about what happened and how to prevent it.
The deepest reason a problem happened, not just its symptoms.
Measuring the speed and errors real users see in their browsers or apps.
Tools that measure how fast an app responds and where it slows down.
Breaking things on purpose to check that a system recovers.
Repetitive manual work that could be automated.
Step-by-step instructions for handling a known problem.
An AI agent that investigates incidents and suggests fixes for engineers.
Computers learning patterns from data instead of following hand-written rules.
An AI model trained on huge amounts of text that can read and write language.
The instructions or question you give to an AI model.
A small piece of text, often part of a word, that an AI model reads.
How much text an AI model can read at once.
When an AI confidently says something that is false.
Extra training of a model on your own examples to make it better at one task.
Using a trained model to get answers, as opposed to training it.
Turning text into a list of numbers that captures its meaning, so similar meanings sit close together.
A list of numbers that stands for something, like the meaning of a sentence.
A database that finds items with similar meaning by comparing embeddings.
Giving an AI relevant documents from a search first, so its answer uses real facts.
Splitting long documents into small pieces so search and AI can use them.
An AI that can plan steps and use tools to finish a task by itself.
An open standard that lets AI agents connect to tools and data.
Rules and checks that stop an AI from doing harmful or wrong things.
Tests that measure how well an AI system does its job.
AI that creates new text, images, code, or sound.
Turning spoken words into written text automatically.
Finding documents that contain the exact words you typed.
Finding results by meaning, even if they use different words.
Combining keyword search and semantic search to get better results.
A classic formula for ranking keyword search results.
A way to merge two ranked result lists into one.
A model that reorders search results so the most relevant come first.
A structure that makes searching data fast, like the list at the back of a book.
A search that runs backwards: stored queries are checked against each new document.
Finding and fetching the most useful pieces of information for a question.
A collection of documents that people or an AI can search to find answers.
A question or search request sent to a database or search engine.
How well a search result matches what the person was looking for.
A specific situation or problem that a product is used to solve.
A product the provider runs and maintains for you, so your team does not operate it.
A popular search engine and database for keyword, semantic, and hybrid search.
